claims.text: The target material is a Ta-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a BCC solid state at 0 K.
A Local-Cluster Perturbation scheme can replace full phase-space thermodynamic integration with a single-step perturbation from a reference solid state to a liquid-like cluster state.
The Moment Tensor Potential is trained on high-temperature liquid snapshots at 1.5–2.0 Tm and BCC solid clusters.
A system size of at least 500 atoms is sufficient to capture local chemical disorder in the proposed simulations.
Transient high-entropy liquid-like clusters form within the BCC lattice and act as nucleation seeds.
The accuracy of the free-energy landscape depends on the MTP capturing species-specific local coordination environments and bond lengths.
An MTP trained on high-temperature liquid data provides a smooth and accurate potential-energy surface for the liquid phase.
Standard EAM potentials fail to capture the complex liquid structure because they rely on pair correlations.
The solid–liquid free-energy difference is dominated by local structural rearrangements rather than long-range collective modes.
Local dominance permits free-energy perturbation over a localized cluster instead of the entire system.
Local-cluster perturbation avoids the claimed exponential scaling of thermodynamic integration.
The proposed method will predict the true melting point within 50 K.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by two orders of magnitude relative to standard TOR-TILD.
The free-energy difference will depend smoothly and monotonically on temperature without hysteresis artifacts.
Standard perturbation methods commonly exhibit hysteresis artifacts.
Standard TOR-TILD requires extensive sampling of the entire phase space, resulting in prohibitively high computational cost and potential inaccuracies in multicomponent systems.
The hypothesis applies to refractory BCC HEAs with atomic-size mismatch greater than 5% and high mixing entropy.
The method may fail for systems with strong directional bonding or extreme chemical segregation because their liquid structures may not be represented by the training set.
Missing electronic effects or solid–liquid interfacial anharmonicity in the MTP may systematically bias the predicted melting point.
The local-cluster approximation may break down in systems with long-range order or specific solute clustering.
